content: Ions such as bromide occur naturally in surface and groundwater, with their levels fluctuating seasonally. Bromide levels can increase due to saltwater intrusion during droughts or from pollution. No guideline value has been established for bromide in drinking water because its concentrations are typically well below levels of health concern. The World Health Organization (WHO) assessed bromide in 2009, concluding that available data were insufficient to derive health-based guideline values. Dibromoacetic acid lacks sufficient data for establishing a guideline value due to the absence of long-term toxicity studies, toxicokinetic studies, carcinogenicity studies, and multigenerational reproductive toxicity studies. Limited mutagenicity data suggest that dibromoacetate is genotoxic. Similarly, data on the oral toxicity of monobromoacetic acid and bromochloroacetic acid are limited, with mixed results for mutagenicity and genotoxicity. These gaps make it impossible to establish guideline values for these chemicals. Cadmium, a metal used in the steel industry and batteries, is released into the environment through wastewater and pollution from fertilizers and air contamination. Drinking water contamination can also occur from impurities in galvanized pipes, solders, and metal fittings. Cadmium accumulates in the kidneys and has a long biological half-life of 10–35 years. The kidney is the primary target organ for cadmium toxicity. The WHO established a provisional tolerable monthly intake (PTMI) of 25 µg/kg body weight due to cadmium's long half-life, replacing the previous weekly intake limit. Carbaryl, a carbamate insecticide, is primarily used in agriculture and public health. It is rarely detected in drinking water unless overspraying or spillage occurs. Carbaryl inhibits brain cholinesterase, its primary mode of toxicity, and is considered a non-genotoxic carcinogen in mice. A guideline value of 0.008 mg/kg body weight was derived based on a lowest-observed-adverse-effect level (LOAEL) of 15 mg/kg/day, applying a safety factor of 2000. However, carbaryl is not typically found in drinking water at significant concentrations, so a formal guideline value is unnecessary. Carbofuran's primary systemic effect is cholinesterase inhibition, with no evidence of teratogenicity, carcinogenicity, or genotoxicity. A guideline value of 1 µg/L is achievable using granular activated carbon (GAC) treatment. Carbon tetrachloride, used in the production of refrigerants and solvents, has decreased in use due to the Montreal Protocol. It is primarily released into the atmosphere but can persist in anaerobic groundwater for extended periods. The liver and kidneys are the main targets of its toxicity. In animal studies, carbon tetrachloride induced liver tumors at high doses, likely secondary to its hepatotoxic effects. It is classified as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B) by IARC. A guideline value of 0.001 mg/L is achievable using air stripping. Chloral hydrate, a by-product of water chlorination, is found in drinking water at concentrations typically below 10 µg/L. It has been used as a sedative in humans at much higher doses than those from drinking water. There is no evidence linking chloral hydrate to cancer in humans, and IARC classifies it as not classifiable regarding carcinogenicity (Group 3). Due to its low concentrations in drinking water, a guideline value is not necessary. Chloramines (monochloramine, dichloramine, and trichloramine) are by-products of water chlorination. Monochloramine is the most abundant and is used as a secondary disinfectant. It is less effective than chlorine but helps maintain residual disinfection in distribution systems. Monochloramine has shown mutagenicity in vitro but not in vivo and is classified as not classifiable regarding carcinogenicity (Group 3) by IARC. Data on dichloramine and trichloramine are insufficient to establish health-based guideline values. Chlordane, a broad-spectrum insecticide, is now primarily used for termite control. It is highly persistent, bioaccumulative, and resistant to degradation. Chlordane is rarely found in groundwater and is classified as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B) by IARC. A guideline value of 1 µg/L is achievable using GAC treatment. Chloride in drinking water originates from natural sources, sewage, industrial effluents, and urban runoff. Excessive chloride concentrations can increase metal corrosion in distribution systems. No health-based guideline value is proposed, but concentrations above 250 mg/L may affect water taste. Chlorine, widely used as a disinfectant, reacts in water to form hypochlorous acid and hypochlorites. It is not associated with specific adverse effects in humans or animals exposed through drinking water. IARC classifies hypochlorite as not classifiable regarding carcinogenicity (Group 3). Chlorine dioxide, used as a disinfectant, decomposes into chlorite and chloride upon ingestion. Chlorite and chlorate are by-products of chlorine dioxide and hypochlorite use. Chlorite primarily affects red blood cells through oxidative stress, while chlorate has similar effects. Provisional guideline values for chlorite and chlorate are 0.7 mg/L and 0.3 mg/L, respectively, with efforts to minimize their concentrations without compromising disinfection. Chloroacetones, formed during water chlorination, are detected at low concentrations in drinking water. Data on their toxicity are insufficient to establish guideline values. Chlorophenols, by-products of phenol chlorination, may also be present in drinking water.
